Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, the **Bregman distance** generated by $\xi^\dagger$ from the reference point $x^\dagger$ to $x$ is

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

The subgradient inequality makes this quantity nonnegative, and $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x^\dagger,x^\dagger)=0$. The definition fixes the orientation: the first argument is the comparison point and the second is the reference point carrying the chosen subgradient.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, let $F:D(F)\subseteq X\to Y$, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex with $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$. Fix $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$, an exponent $1\le p<\infty$, a continuous nondecreasing concave function $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, a coefficient $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0\ge R(x^\dagger)$. The **variational source condition** with these data holds on the named regularizer sublevel $L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}$ when

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad(x\in L_{R_0}).$$

The condition is an assumption on the selected subgradient and the stated sublevel; it makes no assertion that a subgradient exists at every point or that a regularized minimizer exists.

Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing, concave, and satisfy $\psi(0)=0$. Extend $g=-\psi$ to $\mathbb R$ by $g(s)=+\infty$ for $s<0$, and define $H(q):=g^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ for $q>0$, assuming the displayed suprema below are finite. For $c_1,c_2,C_3,\alpha>0$ and $d,r,e\ge0$, if

$$c_1r+c_2\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(C_3r),$$

then

$$e\le\frac1{c_2}\left(\frac d\alpha+H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{C_3\alpha}\right)\right),\qquad r\le\frac2{c_1}\left(d+\alpha H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{2C_3\alpha}\right)\right).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set in the norm topology. A **nonlinear forward model on Hilbert spaces** is a map $F:U\to Y$; no linearity is assumed, and linear maps are allowed as special cases. For $y\in Y$, its exact solution set is

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

A point $x^\dagger\in U$ generates the exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$. When $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$, write $F'(x):X\to Y$ for its unique bounded real-linear derivative.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, let $y\in Y$, and let $x_0\in X$. A point $x^\dagger\in U$ is an **$x_0$-minimum-norm solution** of $F(x)=y$ on $U$ if $F(x^\dagger)=y$ and

$$\|x^\dagger-x_0\|\le\|x-x_0\|\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ with }F(x)=y.$$

This definition asserts no existence or uniqueness; it describes the minimizing property of a supplied exact solution. The minimum is global over the exact solution set on $U$, with distance measured from the specified reference point $x_0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be a nonempty domain, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. For a regularization parameter $\alpha>0$, reference element $x_0\in X$, and datum $y\in Y$, the **nonlinear Tikhonov functional** is the map $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}:D\to[0,\infty)$ defined by

$$
J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x):=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-x_0\|_X^2\qquad(x\in D).
$$

A **global minimizer** is a point $x_\alpha\in D$ such that $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x_\alpha)\le J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)$ for every $x\in D$. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

As $\rho_\delta\to0$ and $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$, $x_\delta\in L_{R_0}$ for sufficiently small $\delta$.

By [F5]–[F7] the special case uses the open-domain Hilbert map, the stipulated global $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, and the existing quadratic nonlinear Tikhonov functional. Under [A6], define $\xi^\dagger(h):=\langle x^\dagger-x_0,h\rangle_X$. By [F10] this is a bounded real-linear functional; expansion using [F9] gives $R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}=\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2\ge0$, so [F1] gives $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$ and [F2] gives $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)=\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2$. Taking $\psi(s)=(\beta_2+1)\sqrt{s}$, the stated Hilbert source inequality implies the VSC with $p=2$.

By [F8], $T_\delta^{1/p}\le r_\delta+\delta$. For $p=1$, $(u+v)^p=u^p+v^p$; for $p>1$, $t\mapsto t^p$ is continuous at zero and has nonnegative second derivative $p(p-1)t^{p-2}$ on $(0,\infty)$, hence is convex on $[0,\infty)$, and its defining convexity inequality at the midpoint gives $(u+v)^p\le2^{p-1}(u^p+v^p)$. Taking $u=r_\delta$, $v=\delta$ yields $T_\delta\le2^{p-1}(r_\delta^p+\delta^p)$ and thus $r_\delta^p/p\ge c_pT_\delta-\delta^p/p$. Substituting into the comparison inequality from 1.1 gives $c_pT_\delta+\alpha(R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger))\le2\delta^p/p+\varepsilon_\delta$.

For $B:=\beta_2+1>0$, the conjugate is $H(q)=\sup_{u\ge0}(Bu-qu^2)=B^2/(4q)$, by completing the square. With $p=2$, $c_p=1/4$, so $\alpha H(c_p/\alpha)=B^2\alpha^2\asymp\delta^2$ and $\rho_\delta=H(c_p/\alpha)=B^2\alpha\asymp\delta$ when $\alpha\asymp\delta$. The scale comparability in [A3] also holds because $H(c_p/(2\alpha))=2H(c_p/\alpha)$.

Fix $1\le p<\infty$, $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$. Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and assume the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad\left(x\in L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}\right),$$

where $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$. Extend $-\psi$ by $+\infty$ on negative arguments and write $H(q):=(-\psi)^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$; assume $H(q)$ is finite for sufficiently large $q$ and $H(q)\to0$ as $q\to\infty$. For sufficiently small noise levels $\delta>0$ and data $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, define $J_\alpha^\delta(x):=p^{-1}\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha R(x)$. Suppose $\alpha=\alpha(\delta)>0$ tends to zero, $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$, and $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in D(F)$ is an $\varepsilon_\delta$-minimizer, meaning $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})\le\inf_{z\in D(F)}J_\alpha^\delta(z)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Set $c_p:=2^{1-p}/p$ and $\rho_\delta:=H(c_p/\alpha(\delta))$. Assume that for constants $c_-,c_+,C_H>0$ independent of $\delta$,

$$c_-\delta^p\le\alpha(\delta)\rho_\delta\le c_+\delta^p,\qquad H(c_p/(2\alpha(\delta)))\le C_H\rho_\delta$$

for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Then for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in L_{R_0}$ and

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon},x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta),\qquad \|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta).$$

If, in addition, $\psi(C_0\delta^p)=O(\rho_\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$ such that $T_\delta:=\|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\le C_0\delta^p$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, then $|R(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If also $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$, then $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$.

In the Hilbert special case, set $p=2$ and suppose $X,Y$ are real Hilbert spaces, $F:U\to Y$ has the real open-domain interface of a nonlinear forward map, $x^\dagger$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, $R(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_X^2$, and the source inequality on a regularizer sublevel contained in $U$ is

$$\langle x^\dagger-x_0,x^\dagger-x\rangle_X\le\beta_1\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2+\beta_2\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y$$

with $0\le\beta_1<1$ and $\beta_2\ge0$. For exact global minimizers of the nonlinear Tikhonov functional with $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta$, the theorem gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$.
